report:
# Do Benzodiazepines Increase Dementia Risk? A Mixed Evidence Base

The evidence is genuinely mixed, and the honest answer is "possibly, but not clearly causal" rather than a confident yes.

**Evidence supporting an association:** Several observational studies have found increased dementia risk with benzodiazepine use. A widely-cited 2012 prospective population-based study in *The BMJ* found new benzodiazepine use was associated with increased dementia risk, robust across cohorts and a case-control analysis (https://www.bmj.com/content/345/bmj.e6231). Multiple meta-analyses of observational studies have reached similar conclusions, including one in *PLOS ONE* finding a dose-response pattern (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0127836).

**Evidence against causation:** However, more methodologically rigorous studies challenge this link. A 2016 *BMJ* study found dementia risk was only slightly elevated with minimal exposure but *not* with the highest exposure levels—inconsistent with a true dose-response causal effect—and concluded results "do not support a causal association" (https://www.bmj.com/content/352/bmj.i90). A 2022 study explicitly designed to address reverse causation found "little evidence of a causal relation between BZD use and dementia risk" (https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/trc2.12309). A recent reanalysis attributed apparent associations to confounding by diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and anxiety, finding the association disappeared with better confounding control (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167494325001086).

**The core problem:** Anxiety, depression, and insomnia—the conditions benzodiazepines treat—are themselves early symptoms of prodromal dementia, creating substantial "reverse causation" bias that is difficult to fully rule out in observational data.

**Conclusion:** The evidence does not clearly establish that benzodiazepines cause dementia. Associations in some studies likely reflect confounding and reverse causation rather than a true causal effect. Regardless, benzodiazepines carry well-established risks (falls, confusion, sedation) warranting caution in older adults independent of dementia risk.
